 ## Search results
NextItNet’s causal dilated-convolution backbone already supports sampled-softmax training; stronger supervision can therefore be explored without changing model family ([original paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf)). Relevant 2024 research finds that sampled softmax implicitly emphasizes hard negatives, but temperature needs tuning: overly low temperatures let a few difficult negatives dominate gradients ([Wu et al.](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf)). Scalable Cross-Entropy uses maximum-inner-product search to select informative catalog outputs efficiently ([RecSys 2024](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5392aca9-0bae-4176-9b3a-a8165957ba26)). For nonuniform or in-batch sampling, proposal correction deserves attention: “Correcting the LogQ Correction” distinguishes the always-present positive from sampled negatives and derives an uncertainty-weighted correction. This addresses sampling bias, not false-negative identification ([RecSys 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331)).

False-negative safeguards argue against blindly selecting the highest-scoring unseen items. EMM (2026) combines refreshed hard-negative candidates with random negatives, excludes positive/self IDs, and filters candidates through a similarity window; its reported experiments concern graph recommenders, so transfer to NextItNet remains unverified ([paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026004090)). A practical single-model hypothesis is to warm up with uniform negatives, then mix random candidates with moderately hard candidates scored by the same NextItNet, excluding known training positives and testing conservative weighting of suspiciously similar items. Similarity is only a heuristic for latent relevance. Compare against uniform sampled softmax under the fixed macro validation HR@10 protocol: negative-sampling studies report dataset-dependent accuracy and popularity tradeoffs, so improved training margins alone do not establish gains ([2024 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)).

---

NextItNet’s foundation is stacked dilated causal convolutions with residual connections, expanding receptive fields while preserving sequence order. The searches did not identify a directly matching 2024–2026 NextItNet paper demonstrating learned dilation plus time-aware intent gating. Related evidence supports selective context: GAT4Rec (2024) uses a GRU-derived gate to select informative subsequences; ConvRec (2026) progressively aggregates neighboring interactions through hierarchical convolution. These motivate adaptive context selection but do not establish gains for a gated NextItNet. Sources: [NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163), [GAT4Rec](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7390/12/14/2189/html), [ConvRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04723).

A compatible experimental hypothesis is to retain NextItNet’s causal residual backbone and add jointly trained gates over convolutional features at several fixed dilations. Condition gates on causal hidden states and observed timestamp gaps, allowing recent coherent interactions to dominate while retaining useful older context. This is an inference from related work, not a published or validated result. ScaleRec (2026) provides adjacent motivation through multi-scale preference modeling and adaptive suppression of redundant interactions, although its backbone is Transformer-based. Evaluate gated dilation first, then timestamp conditioning, using the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10 protocol. Keep one jointly trained model/checkpoint per category, final-nonpadding readout, and identical training/predictor architectures. Source: [ScaleRec](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306457325002596).

---

Recent results support text-aware sequential recommendation, but do not establish the exact combination of a from-scratch text encoder, NextItNet, and learned complement/substitute distinctions. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) combines textual item representations with sequential learning, but uses pretrained BERT, a SASRec-derived backbone, and unavailable reviews; its reported gains therefore cannot be assumed under this task’s constraints. [LLM2Rec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21579) similarly emphasizes adapting language representations to collaborative recommendation signals, rather than learning text embeddings from scratch.

[NextItNet](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf) supplies the relevant backbone: residual dilated causal convolutions trained for next-item prediction. A constraint-compatible hypothesis is to jointly train randomly initialized token embeddings and a small title/description encoder, fuse its output with item-ID embeddings inside one NextItNet, and optimize the entire network through next-item loss. This is a proposed adaptation, not a verified result from the retrieved papers. Separate learned history and candidate projections could allow directional associations without forcing textually similar products to receive similar scores.

The [2024 complementary-recommendation survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16135) distinguishes asymmetric complementarity from substitution and discusses their coexistence. Consequently, broad textual similarity should not be treated as a compatibility label. Available histories can supervise observed next-item transitions, but cannot establish that a transition reflects functional complementarity.
